abstract.p: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. Prominent candidate targets include transcription factors (TF), signaling components, raffinose biosynthesis genes implicated in freezing tolerance, regulators of salt and alkaline stress, and determinants of heavy metal tolerance and sequestration. Translational challenges, such as off-target effects, low transformation efficiencies, and editing multiple homologues or haplotypes, are being addressed such as DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, high-throughput screening, haplotype-specific target design, and haplotype-aware guide RNA engineering based on unique genetic variation sites across different gene haplotypes. Collectively, the integration of advanced CRISPR toolkits with enhanced genomic information resources and phenotyping capabilities holds significant potential for accelerating the development of precision-bred, multi-stress-resilient sugar crops that sustain yield, quality, and industrial value under abiotic stress conditions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sugar crops, such as sugarcane (Saccharum hybrid spp.), sugar beet (Beta vulgaris var. saccharifera), and sweet sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) are integral to global agriculture and serve as major sources of sucrose, bioenergy, and various industrial products. A defining attribute of these crops is the accumulation of high sucrose in specialized sink tissues (Kumar et al., 2014; 2024; Pandey et al., 2025). However, the productivity and sustainability of these sugar crops face significant challenges owing to abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity, extreme temperatures (both heat and cold), and heavy metal toxicity. Sugarcane produces approximately 80% of the world’s sugar and is a cornerstone of bioethanol and bioproducts, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions (Pandey et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). Sugar beets, mainly grown in temperate regions, are distinguished by tuberous roots and higher sugar content (Nap et al., 2025). Although sugar beet cultivation incurs higher costs and industrial use offers substantial potential for achieving higher ethanol yields than other feedstocks. To boost sugar beet productivity and ensure quality, it is vital to enhance abiotic and biotic stresses, such as disease resistance, high yield, and sugar content (Abu-Ellail et al., 2024; 2025; Nap et al., 2025). Sweet sorghum is a bioenergy and bioethanol crop known for its wide adaptability to harsh environments. Its minimal water and fertilizer requirements render it well-suited for cultivation on marginal lands, providing a sustainable alternative to maize crops. However, chilling stress constrains the adaptability of crops to cooler climates (Appiah-Nkansah et al., 2019; Yang J. et al., 2025). Genome-editing technologies can further augment this potential by enhancing cold tolerance and reducing agricultural inputs (Maulana and Tesso, 2013). These advancements could facilitate the production of value-added products, thereby broadening the commercial applications of sweet sorghum (Hossain et al., 2022; Ameen et al., 2024).

As climate change intensifies abiotic stress, enhancing stress resilience while maintaining or increasing sucrose accumulation is a critical challenge for sugar crops. Traditional breeding faces significant difficulties due to the polygenic and polyploid nature of the sugarcane genome (∼10 Gb). Numerous sequencing initiatives have targeted both parental species and hybrid genotypes. Notably, haplotype separation and assembly produced high-quality haplotype-resolved assemblies and graph pangenomes for sugarcane. These resources enable gene discovery, genomic selection, and precision editing, thereby overcoming key breeding bottlenecks. Advances in genomic resources for sugar beet and sweet sorghum likewise create new opportunities for precision breeding. These genomic resources summarized in (Supplementary Table S1) have been instrumental in advancing sugar crop improvement. For sugarcane, haplotype-resolved assemblies and graph pangenomes have enabled the identification of stress-responsive gene haplotypes for CRISPR targeting. For sugar beet, reference genomes and pangenome resources have facilitated the discovery of genes associated with salt and cold tolerance. For sweet sorghum, the telomere-to-telomere genome assembly provides a foundation for precise gRNA design. Collectively these genomic resources directly support the CRISPR-based strategies discussed in this review by enabling haplotype-aware gRNA design and functional validation of target genes. Genome editing using CRISPR/Cas systems has revolutionized plant biotechnology by enabling precise and efficient genetic modification. Tools for genome editing, including zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs), transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs), and CRISPR/Cas systems (Figure 1A), provide enhanced simplicity and scalability via RNA-guided DNA recognition. These technologies have broadened the scope for manipulating complex traits in sugar crops, such as abiotic stress tolerance (Zhang et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2024; Pacesa et al., 2024). The application of CRISPR/Cas technology allows for the identification and editing of genes related to drought, salinity, chilling, and heavy metal tolerance, thereby enabling sugar crops to endure adverse environmental conditions while maintaining productivity.

sec.p: The integration of CRISPR/Cas tools into sugar crop breeding programs offers unprecedented opportunities to develop resilient varieties that can withstand various abiotic stressors. Genome editing offers a promising strategy to accelerate the development of stress-resilient sugar crops and support sustainable agriculture under abiotic stress.

sec.title: Overview of Genome editing
sec.p: CRISPR has emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing abiotic tolerance. Genome editing improves drought, salinity, and heat tolerance by targeting genes, such as aquaporins, heat shock proteins, and ion transporters (Nagaraju et al., 2019). Previous studies have demonstrated that the overexpression of specific genes and transcription factors enhances stress tolerance by augmenting the accumulation of signaling molecules (Zhang et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2024; Pacesa et al., 2024; Pandey et al., 2025). Key TF’s families that regulate downstream genes involved in osmo-protection and stomatal regulation, such as the WRKY gene family, specific transcription factors, and the NAC family, no apical meristem (NAM), and dehydration-responsive element binding (DREB). CRISPR-based technologies, including CRISPRa and CRISPRi, offer valuable tools for regulating stress tolerance (Figures 1A–D), and genes in sugar crops (Osakabe et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2018; 2024). Specifically, targeting drought-responsive genes using CRISPR/Cas12a holds promise for enhancing water retention and stress tolerance. CRISPR/Cas systems provide a practical approach to breeding resilient crops capable of overcoming both biotic and abiotic challenges and the development of sugar crop varieties that withstand increasing abiotic stresses induced by climate change (Yolcu et al., 2021). Genome editing encompasses genetic modification that enables precise manipulation of DNA through insertion, deletion, and replacement within plant genomes. Molecular tools, such as ZFNs, TALENs, and (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), significantly advanced plant genetics (Figures 1A–D). These technologies have been rapidly employed to enhance crop yield, improve nutritional quality, and increase resistance to abiotic and biotic stressors (Kumar et al., 2024; Li and Iqbal, 2024; Mall et al., 2024).

Genome editing tools utilize sequence-specific nucleases to recognize and bind to specific DNA sequences, inducing double-stranded breaks (DSBs). ZFNs are customizable DNA-cleaving proteins engineered to target and cleave specific locations. TALENs induce DSBs at designated sites, activating DNA repair response pathways that result in genome modifications. In the CRISPR-Cas9 system, the RNA-guided endonuclease Cas9 employs a guide RNA (gRNA) to recognize and bind to a specific target DNA sequence (protospacer) that is adjacent to a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM). Upon binding, Cas9 introduces a double-strand break (DSB) at the target site (Zhang et al., 2020; Hussain et al., 2021). Specifically, the Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex, comprising the Cas9 endonuclease and guide RNA (gRNA), recognizes and binds to the target sequence through complementary base pairing between the gRNA and gDNA.

Typically, two mechanisms exist for DSB repair. The first mechanism, non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ), results in insertions or deletions (Indels). If these indels induce frameshift mutations (the length is not a multiple of three base pairs), can lead to loss-of-function mutations. The second mechanism, homology-directed repair (HDR), utilizes a donor DNA template with high sequence homology to the regions flanking the DSB to accurately repair the break (Figures 1B,C), potentially correcting existing mutations and enabling precise genetic editing (Hussain et al., 2021; Li and Iqbal, 2024; Mall et al., 2024). In addition to DSB-mediated editing, CRISPR systems can be adapted for transcriptional regulation without permanent DNA modification. CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) utilizes a catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9) fused to transcriptional activation domains, such as VP64 and EDLL, to enhance target gene expression (Figure 1D). In contrast, CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) uses catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9) to repress target gene transcription, either by sterically hindering transcription or by recruiting transcriptional repressor domains such as KRAB. Conversely, CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) couples dCas9 to transcriptional activators to enhance the expression of target genes. Together, CRISPRi and CRISPRa enable programmable modulation of gene expression without permanently altering the underlying DNA sequence, providing complementary strategies for dissecting and engineering stress-responsive pathways. (Ben-Tov et al., 2024).

The CRISPR/Cas system has significant advantages over ZFNs and TALENs because of its simplicity in design, cost-effectiveness, versatility, and efficiency. This approach allows the rapid introduction of guide RNAs to target nearly any DNA sequence with a nearby PAM, facilitating the simultaneous editing of multiple genes through multiplexing (Urnov et al., 2010; Hussain et al., 2021). By employing ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) for direct delivery into plant cells, the CRISPR/Cas system can mitigate the regulatory and public acceptance challenges associated with transgenic or genetically modified (GM) approaches in certain regions, particularly when RNPs are used to avoid foreign DNA integration. This system streamlines the creation of genetically edited plants and expedites development and adoption for future commercial cultivation (Antony Ceasar and Ignacimuthu, 2023). Consequently, enhances crop traits more efficiently and sustains food security in global challenges.

sec.title: Enhancing abiotic stress tolerance by CRISPR/Cas
Abiotic stress challenges
sec.p: Abiotic stresses, particularly those related to climate change, are the most critical constraints on sugar crop productivity worldwide. These stresses frequently occur concurrently under field conditions, resulting in complex stress conditions that exacerbate cellular damage through oxidative stress, membrane destabilization, protein denaturation, and metabolic imbalance (Figure 2). In sugar crops, these stresses not only diminish biomass accumulation but also disrupt sucrose synthesis, transport, and storage, ultimately affecting both yield and quality (Mall et al., 2024; Pandey et al., 2025). Unlike monogenic traits, abiotic stress tolerance is governed by intricate networks of genes involved in various physiological processes, such as signaling pathways, transcriptional regulation, osmotic adjustment, antioxidant defense response, hormone crosstalk, and metabolic reprogramming (Misra et al., 2023; Mall et al., 2024).

caption.p: Schematic overview of climate change-driven abiotic stresses and cascading effects on cellular integrity, sucrose metabolism, and productivity in sugar crops. Major abiotic stresses induced by climate change—including heat stress, drought stress, cold stress, salinity stress, alkalinity stress, and heavy metal stress. These stresses trigger cellular damage through oxidative stress (↑ROS, H2O2, O2 −) membrane destabilization, protein denaturation (misfolding, aggregation), and metabolic imbalance (inhibited enzymes, ATP depletion). Consequently, sucrose metabolism is disrupted through inhibited synthesis (↓SPS activity), transport (↓SUT activity, phloem loading), and storage (↓invertase activity). The cumulative impact results in reduced biomass, sucrose content, and purity, leading to compromised productivity, economic losses, and threats to food security. SciDraw. (2026). sec.p: A primary challenge in enhancing abiotic stress tolerance in plants is the polygenic and quantitative nature of stress-responsive traits. Consequently, traditional breeding relies on phenotypic selection, which is often slow, imprecise, and inefficient, particularly in the genomic architecture of sugarcane and sugar crops.

CRISPR/Cas-based genome-editing technologies are a transformative solution that facilitates the precise and targeted modification of key stress-responsive genes and regulatory elements. By directly manipulating master/hub regulators, signaling components, and metabolic genes associated with abiotic stress tolerance, CRISPR/Cas systems offer unparalleled opportunities to elucidate stress mechanisms and engineer sugar crop varieties with enhanced resilience and productivity under environmental conditions (Misra et al., 2023; Pandey et al., 2025). Understanding the regulation of gene expression in response to drought, salinity, and temperature stress is crucial for developing resilient sugar beet varieties. Manipulating the expression of specific stress-responsive genes in sugar beets under adverse conditions will elucidate the regulatory mechanisms and facilitate the breeding of stress-tolerant sugar beet varieties. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas12a recognizes dsDNA targets bearing a T-rich PAM, upon activation, exhibits non-specific trans-cleavage of ssDNA. For genome editing in sugar crops, Cas12a is utilized for its precise dsDNA cleavage and T-rich PAM compatibility, enabling multiplexed gene knockouts.By targeting genes involved in specific abiotic stress responses, genome editing can enhance the ability of sugar beet to withstand adverse environmental conditions (Figure 2; Table 1). For example, targeting drought-responsive genes using the CRISPR/Cas12a system can significantly improve drought tolerance in plants. These genetically modified plants demonstrated enhanced water retention capabilities, reduced wilting, and increased tolerance under drought conditions. Consequently, the utilization of CRISPR/Cas technology is vital for breeding highly resilient sugar crop varieties that can combat biotic and abiotic stress (Figures 1, 2). The application of CRISPR/Cas technology involves specific procedures for cultivating sugar crop varieties with diverse abiotic stress tolerance (Tables 1–3) respectively.

sec.title: Enhancing tolerance to drought, cold, and heat stresses
sec.p: Sugar crops are significantly affected by various stresses that alter morphological, physiological, biochemical, and molecular characteristics (Pandey et al., 2025; Wang Z. et al., 2026). These stresses adversely affect the yield, growth, and development, causing physical damage and physiological disruption. Molecular non-specific lipid transfer proteins (nsLTPs) play a crucial role in facilitating lipid transport across cellular membranes as a plant-adaptive mechanism to drought stress (Table 2). In response to drought stress, plants upregulated the expression of nsLTP genes (Figures 3A,B). These proteins contribute to membrane integrity and stability by transferring lipids between membranes, thereby reducing water loss through transpiration and cellular dehydration (Liu et al., 2015; Giri and Kumar, 2026).

sec.p: Heat stress disrupts membrane and protein folding, leading to cell damage. nsLTPs have also been implicated in thermotolerance by stabilizing the membranes at high temperatures (Chen et al., 2017; Hussain et al., 2018). S. spontaneum produces soluble, small basic proteins (ScNsLTPs) involved in drought adaptive responses (Hussain et al., 2018). The ScNsLTP gene validated with upregulation under chilling and PEG stress, represents a high-priority target for CRISPRa-mediated overexpression to improve drought and cold resilience ((Chen et al., 2017; Li and Iqbal, 2024). The transcript of the LTPL24 gene in S. bicolor, belongs to non-specific lipid transfer proteins, increases drought resistance in the presence of polyethylene glycol (PEG) (Abdel-Ghany et al., 2020). This suggests that genes encoding non-specific lipid transfer proteins can be targeted by the CRISPR/Cas system in sugar crops to develop drought tolerance (Table 3). Furthermore, the IWF5 protein, consisting of 92 amino acids, was isolated from sugar beet leaf intercellular fluid using cation-exchange chromatography and reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography. NsLTP has eight conserved cysteine residues in its amino acid sequence (Kristensen et al., 2000). The advent of CRISPR/Cas base editors presents a promising opportunity to enhance the utility of IWF5 in conferring valuable traits, such as drought and heat resistance, to sugar crops (Table 1).

Numerous TFs, including members of the v-myb avian myeloblastosis viral oncogene homologue (MYB) family and bZIP proteins, associated with resilience against stressors. Genes within the myeloblastosis (MYB) family are crucial for orchestrating plant responses to various abiotic stressors (Jiang et al., 2017). These TFs function as master regulators, modulating gene expression networks involved in stress perception, signal transduction, and subsequent physiological adaptations (Figures 3B,C). For example, Sb08g019720.1, associated with the SNP-8-50726311 locus, exhibits homology with the Arabidopsis EFM gene, a member of the MYB family of transcription factors. Similarly, Sb01g037050.1, linked to the SNP-1-60603003 locus, is homologous to a maize gene encoding a basic leucine zipper (bZIP). These findings suggest that the early flowering MYB protein (EFM) and bZIP genes play a significant role in the drought tolerance of sweet sorghum. These genes can be edited using CRISPR/Cas tools to enhance drought tolerance (Table 3). Similarly, the promoter of the S. officinarum stress-related MYB (ScMYBAS1) has been identified, which regulates abiotic stresses such as dehydration, salt, cold, and hormone treatments salicylic acid (SA) and methyl jasmonate) (Prabu and Theertha Prasad, 2012). Therefore, engineering the PScMYBAS1 gene in sugar crops using CRISPRa can enhance tolerance to stress conditions.

In sugarcane, genes from S. spontaneum jasmonate zim domain 1/2/3/4 (SsJAZ1-1/2/3/4) were significantly upregulated under drought conditions. The transcript level of ScJAZ1 was elevated in response to jasmonic acid (JA), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and abscisic acid (ABA). These genes are crucial candidates for sugarcane breeding, providing a foundation for enhancing drought stress tolerance (Table 2), through targeted gene modifications (Zhou et al., 2024). However, studies on ScD27.2’s role in drought-mediated tillering plasticity coordinates with the transcription factor ScMYB44, revealing a molecular module integrating strigolactone metabolism, plant architecture, and stress adaptation (Zan et al., 2023; Wu Z. et al., 2026). RNAi-mediated knockdown of ScD27.2 increases tiller number and reduces drought tolerance, while overexpression suppresses tillering and enhances drought tolerance. A CRISPR/Cas9 knockout would phenocopy the RNAi knockdown line, resulting in increased tillering but compromised drought tolerance, which is the opposite of the desired outcome for enhancing drought resilience. Therefore, CRISPRa-mediated overexpression of ScD27.2 represents the appropriate strategy to enhance drought tolerance while reducing tillering. Alternatively, promoter editing or base editing could be employed to achieve more subtle modulation of ScD27.2 expression, potentially uncoupling the trade-off between tillering and stress tolerance. Similarly, B. vulgaris BvMYB genes, such as Bv Rapid alkalization factor (ralf) and Bv_jkkr, have shown targets for CRISPR/Cas editing, indicating a pathway for precise genetic modifications in sugar beet to enhance drought resistance (Stracke et al., 2014).

Genes associated with heat shock factors (HSFs) responded to heat stress (Figures 3B,C). HSFs activate the transcription of heat shock genes, including heat shock proteins (HSPs), which are essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and protecting plants against stress-induced damage. In sugarcane, heat stress induces HSF genes, particularly members of the HSF-A and HSF-B classes, whereas BvHSF genes in sugar beet are responsive to both heat and salt stresses. These stress-responsive HSFs therefore represent potential targets for genetic manipulation to enhance abiotic stress resilience in sugar crops. (Ismail et al., 2020; Zhang J.-L. et al., 2024). The CRISPRa system employs dCas9 fused to transcriptional activator domains (e.g., VP64) to upregulate BvHSF expression without inducing DNA breaks, potentially enhancing heat resistance. Moreover, transcriptomic analyses revealed upregulation of HSF genes in sweet sorghum under heat stress. Using the CRISPR/Cas system, targeted editing of the SbHsp70-1 gene in sweet sorghum can improve heat resistance (Mulaudzi-Masuku et al., 2015; Misra et al., 2023). The heat- and drought-inducible- activities of heterologous sHSP promoters, particularly stems, correlate with the native expression and water stress-response of endogenous class I small HSP genes, supporting the conserved role of HSP-mediated-regulatory networks in sugarcane stress adaptation. Similarly, SsHsp17.2 and SsHsp17.9, classified as class I Hsps, expressed in vitro in sugarcane. Furthermore, the SsHsp17.2 gene is induced in sugarcane under water stress (Tiroli and Ramos, 2007; Tiroli-Cepeda and Ramos, 2010; Qiande and Altpeter, 2025). Genes encoding small heat shock proteins, including SsHsp17.2 and SsHsp17.9, have been validated at the transcriptional level in sugarcane (Tiroli and Ramos, 2007; Tiroli-Cepeda and Ramos, 2010; Qiande and Altpeter, 2025). CRISPRa-mediated activation of these genes represents a promising strategy to enhance heat-stress resilience. Furthermore, the DREB-family plays a pivotal role in conferring drought tolerance (Figure 3) (Zhang and Xia, 2023). In a recent investigation, 30 BvDREB family genes were classified into six distinct subfamilies in sugar beets. The BvDREB genes were responsive to drought stress and exhibited varying expression patterns. These findings contribute to drought tolerance by regulating ABA signaling pathways, proline biosynthesis, and hormone levels (Qiu et al., 2024). Similarly, 11-DREB1/CBF genes in cold-tolerant Erianthus fulvus confirmed cold-responsive genes, and validated that EfDREB1C acts as a nuclear transcriptional activator enhancing cold tolerance (Qian et al., 2025), by regulating multiple stress-related pathways, providing gene targets for sugarcane cold resistance. Collectively, these findings represent promising targets for gene editing using the CRISPR/Cas system to enhance the abiotic tolerance of sugar crops.

Worldwide, crops are subjected to severe cold spells and simultaneously face drought conditions or impaired water transport and absorption during the cold season. The simultaneous occurrence of chilling and drought stress substantially hinders plant development and poses a significant threat to crop yields (Chan et al., 2025; Yanqing et al., 2026). These stressors severely affect the yield, growth, and development of sugar crops, leading to morphological, physiological, and biochemical changes, as well as molecular modifications (Figures 2, 3). Taken together, nsLTPs are indispensable components of plant defense mechanisms against adverse stress. Transcript analysis revealed the upregulation of the ScNsLTP gene under chilling and PEG stress in sugarcane, indicating a stress response to low temperatures (Chen et al., 2017). Genome-wide investigations have identified 71 nsLTP genes in Saccharum spp. that exhibit distinct expression patterns in response to salicylic acid treatment (Li J. et al., 2022), providing gene targets for improving stress tolerance in sugarcane. The SsGF2.1–2.4 family genes were identified to be expressed in various tissues in response to cold stress (Zhang H.-L. et al., 2024). These genes belong to the 14-3-3 protein family, a group of highly conserved acidic proteins in sugarcane. In S. bicolor, two NsLTP genes, SbLTP1.4 and SbLTP1.5, exhibit distinct floral tissue–specific and stress-responsive promoters (Cossio et al., 2025), suitable for driving efficient CRISPR-mediated genome editing.

The reduced expression of BvLTP-1 is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction under cold stress in sugar beet (Matsuhira et al., 2007). CRISPRa could be employed to restore or enhance BvLTP-1 expression, thereby preserving mitochondrial function and improving chilling tolerance. Alternatively, may dominant-negative isoform is responsible, base editing could correct the regulatory variant. In sugar beet, increased raffinose accumulation in the root pith contributes to freezing tolerance, highlighting the protective role of raffinose under cold stress. Raffinose-family oligosaccharides (RFOs) are also important for cold acclimation, with galactinol synthase (GOLS) acting as a key regulator of their biosynthesis and representing a potential target for genetic manipulation.(Keller et al., 2021). The isolation and characterization of BvRS1 and BvRS2, genes encoding raffinose synthase (RS), a key enzyme showed that chilling stress induces transcription in leaves and roots (Kito et al., 2017). High expression of GOLS2, GOLS3, BvRS2, and BvRS5 has been observed under cold conditions (Keller et al., 2021). Notably, the BvRS5 gene and raffinose content showed significant increases during freezing in taproots of tolerant sugar beet varieties, indicating enhanced expression of GOLS and RS genes, for freezing resistance (Keller et al., 2021; Yolcu et al., 2021; Pandey et al., 2025). Consequently, targeting GOLS and RS genes using CRISPRa (dCas9-transcriptional activator fusion) may enhance the resistance of sugar beet varieties to freezing stress by upregulating raffinose biosynthesis without introducing permanent genomic alterations. Notably, membrane proteins are crucial for detecting cold stress and initiating cytosolic Ca+2 signals, which may regulate downstream transcription factors.

Squamous promoter-binding protein (SPL) transcription factors play a crucial role in regulating plant growth and development. BvSPL6 expresses mature roots under abiotic stress. Similarly, BvSPL3 in sugar beets enhances resistance to cold. BvSPL3 contributes to root growth and sugar accumulation. The CRISPR-Cas system allows the targeting of these genes to improve cold stress in sugar beets. By editing the BvSPL6 and BvSPL3 genes using CRISPRa, their expression can be enhanced, thereby increasing plant resilience to cold stress. For example, overexpression of BvSPL6 could enhance root development and cold stress, and modification of BvSPL3 could optimize root growth and sugar accumulation during plant maturation. Targeted genetic interventions using the CRISPR/Cas system can significantly enhance the overall cold tolerance and productivity of sugar beets through the inherent functions of SPL genes (Xue et al., 2024). In sweet sorghum, SbCBF6 exhibited increased expression levels during chilling stress. The regulation of CBF expression is modulated by JA signaling. Notably, in chilling-tolerant sorghum, key genes involved in JA biosynthesis, such as allene oxidase synthase and 12-oxophytodienoic acid reductase, were upregulated. This finding indicates that JA biosynthesis plays a crucial role in imparting chilling tolerance (Chopra et al., 2015; Marla et al., 2017; Namata et al., 2025). Additionally, a massively parallel reporter assay was employed to systematically evaluate 30,000 CRISPR-accessible mutations, including deletions, substitutions, and motif insertions, across the native promoters and 5′untranslated regions of three photosynthesis genes; PsbS, Raf1, and SBPase. These results showed that gene expression is modulated within a ∼500-bp core promoter region, with mutational effects that are reproducible and protein accumulation. Notably, compact deletions and targeted motif insertions in these regions enhanced protein production 30-fold- relative to the wild type (Groover et al., 2026). Since mutation-effect-relationships were gene-specific. These findings highlight the need for customized regulatory maps. Thus, a high-throughput-cis-regulatory fine-mapping-approach enables targeted, minimal, and non-transgenic CRISPR edits to advance the improvement of sugar crops.

sec.title: Improving saline and alkaline stress tolerance
sec.p: Salinity presents significant challenges to sugar crops, leading to hyperosmotic and ionic imbalances that affect crop production, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions (Figure 4). ScGluD2, a novel member of the subfamily D beta-1,3-glucanase, acts as a stress-responsive gene in sugarcane and is expressed as a defense mechanism against smut fungi and saline stress (Wu et al., 2022). The expression of ScGluD2 transcripts increased after 12 h of salt stress. The transcripts were upregulated between 6 and 24 h following ABA, H2O2, and CdCl2 treatment, indicating that ABA may function as a signaling molecule regulating oxidative stress and play a pivotal role under salt stress (Su et al., 2016). ScGluD2 transcript upregulated under salt stress can be targeted for CRISPRa-mediated overexpression to confer saline stress resistance in sugarcane. Various TF family genes, such as WRKY, NAC, and MYB have been identified to contribute to abiotic stress tolerance (Zhang et al., 2022). Under saline-alkaline conditions, WRKY family genes can be activated through CRISPRa activation or downregulated via CRISPRi interference, targeting genes involved in stress responses and mitigating the adverse effects of stress on plants. Additionally, WRKY (TFs) enhance the antioxidant defense system of plants by regulating genes encoding antioxidant enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and peroxidases (POD) (Zhang et al., 2022; Zeng et al., 2024; Yang L. et al., 2025). The detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS) protects plant cells from oxidative damage (Figures 3C, 4). These genes can also regulate the expression of osmolyte biosynthesis genes, leading to the accumulation of proline, glycine, betaine, and sugars (Zeng et al., 2024). These compounds contribute to osmotic adjustment and cellular protection, while coordinated regulation of ion transport systems maintains ion homeostasis by promoting the retention and compartmentalization of essential ions such as K+ and the exclusion or sequestration of toxic ions.

Crop-specific targets: sugarcane (ScGluD2, ScWRKY5); sugar beet (BvWRKY10/16, BvbHLH93); sweet sorghum (SbWRKY50, NADP-ME, SbBADH2). sec.p: Elevated pH levels in alkaline soils disrupt cellular pH stability, cell membrane integrity, and reduce root vigor and photosynthetic activity in sugar beets. Under saline stress, cultivated sugar beet varieties exhibit increased antioxidant enzyme activity (Wang et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; Rao et al., 2023). Homeostasis of K+ and Na+ is a critical adaptation strategy for sugar beets under alkaline stress (Houmani and Corpas, 2026). The identification of 58 WRKY genes, nine of which respond to alkaline stress in sugar beet shoots and roots. Elevated expression of BvWRKY10 (in terminal and lateral shoots) and BvWRKY16 (in roots) under alkaline stress. A significant increase in Na+ concentration in the shoots and roots of sugar beets under alkaline conditions, increasing sodium bicarbonate concentrations; keeping, potassium ion concentrations stable (Wu et al., 2019a). Manipulation of BvWRKY gene expression using CRISPR/Cas tools may yield stress-resistant sugar beet varieties (Table 1). These genes play pivotal roles in sugar beet development and alkaline stress.

Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) and bHLH genes in sugar beets respond to alkaline and salt stress, respectively. For example, BvbHLH93 mitigates reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and regulates polyamine metabolism during salt stress (Wang Y. et al., 2021). Similarly, the expression of Sporisorium scitamineum ScWRKY5 is significantly altered in response to various stressors, including inoculation, salicylic acid, abscisic acid, polyethylene glycol, and sodium chloride (Wang et al., 2020). Notably, after inoculation with S. scitamineum, resistant sugarcane varieties exhibited increased ScWRKY5 expression, whereas susceptible varieties showed decreased expression. CRISPRa technology can be used to edit ScWRKY5 by targeting specific regions to enhance its activity under saline and alkaline stress. The responsiveness of plants to these stresses can be augmented by introducing mutations or modifications through base or prime editing, thereby improving the resilience and productivity of sugarcane under saline and alkaline conditions.

SbWRKY50 from sweet sorghum negatively influences salt stress responses in A. thaliana by regulating ion homeostasis by binding to the upstream promoter of SOS1 and HKT1 genes, thereby offering valuable insights into enhancing saline stress tolerance in sweet sorghum using the CRISPR/Cas system (Song et al., 2020). Conversely, NAC may modulate the expression of genes involved in osmotic adjustment, ion uptake and compartmentalization, maintenance of cell integrity, and stress signaling pathways. In sweet sorghum, the non-functional gene, NAC074A, has been linked to increased juice yield, thereby increasing the overall sugar content. However, genetic variation did not alter the sucrose concentration or Brix of the juice. Instead, resulted in a higher total juice volume per plant (Xia et al., 2018). This led to a greater total amount of sucrose per plant, enhancing the value of the plant for sugar production. This gene can be targeted using CRISPRa to increase the overall sugar productivity of sweet sorghum under abiotic stress (Table 3).

In sugar beet salt-tolerant cultivars, the expression of NAC21, NAC22, and NAC100, were targets of miR164, exclusively induced under salt stress (Cui et al., 2018). Moreover, NAC family genes involved in stress response regulation using CRISPR/Cas technology could be highly beneficial for enhancing tolerance to salt and alkaline stress in sweet sorghum, sugarcane, and sugar beet plants. Through precise gene editing, researchers can elucidate the specific roles and regulatory mechanisms of NAC (TFs) in plant stress adaptation, thereby improving the yield, stability, and productivity. MYB (TFs), may regulate the expression of genes involved in osmolyte synthesis, stomatal closure, hormonal signaling, and metabolic adjustments to enhance stress tolerance (Wu et al., 2024). Gene expression patterns related to salt resistance in sweet sorghum identified MYB-type TFs as specific to salt-tolerant sorghum varieties. These MYB-type TFs are crucial for the synthesis of secondary metabolites and environmental stress (Chen et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2025). The diverse expression profiles of MYB-type TFs may contribute to variations in gene response patterns associated with secondary metabolite synthesis in salt-tolerant sorghum genotypes. Investigating the regulatory mechanisms of these genes using CRISPRa or CRISPRi systems could enhance the salt and alkaline stress tolerance of sugar beets and sweet sorghum. Similarly, salt stress upregulates the gene encoding NADP-dependent- malic enzyme (NADP-ME) in sweet sorghum (Guo et al., 2018). This increases CO2 and pyruvate levels, boosting CO2 fixation efficiency, whereas it produced NADPH supports ROS detoxification (Mittler et al., 2022). Targeted editing of NADP-ME genes using CRISPR/Cas technologies offers a promising strategy to improve photosynthetic performance, salt tolerance and productivity in sugar crops under saline conditions.

The gene Sb04g030640, associated with ABA synthesis in sweet sorghum, was upregulated in the leaves. In addition, genes involved in the ABA signaling pathway, such as pyrabactin resistance (PYR)/pyrabactin resistance-like (PYL) and type 2C protein phosphatase (PP2C), exhibited distinct expression patterns. Specifically, the PYL8-encoding gene Sb09g006700 was downregulated in the roots of the salt-sensitive line, whereas PP2C-encoding, gene were upregulated in the salt-sensitive line but downregulated in the salt-tolerant line of sweet sorghum (Yang et al., 2017). CRISPR/Cas tools can be used to fine-tune the expression of genes involved in the synthesis and signaling of jasmonic acid (JA), indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), and cytokinins (CK), thereby ensuring optimal hormonal balance and stress response. These genetic modifications can collectively improve the resilience of sweet sorghum to saline environments and enhance its growth and productivity. In contrast, the downregulation of genes encoding light-harvesting proteins, specifically Lhca1 and Lhcb1-5, is associated with enhanced salt stress tolerance in sweet sorghum plants. Moreover, genes encoding Lhca2-4 and Lhcb6 are integral for controlling tolerance to saline conditions. Additionally, the upregulation of Sb02g002830 and Sb09g021810 is crucial for the stable assembly of the oxygen-evolving complex and ATP synthase, respectively, and contributes to the stability of the photosynthetic system during salt stress (Sui et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020). Taken together, these genes are potential targets for CRISPRa tools to enhance salt stress tolerance in sweet sorghum.

sec.title: Heavy metal stress tolerance
sec.p: The exposure of plants to toxic heavy metals induces a range of metabolic and physiological changes that are contingent upon the concentration of these metals in the soil and specific plant species and varieties (Sperdouli, 2022; Ghuge et al., 2023). The development of sugar crops with enhanced tolerance to heavy metal stress is essential to sustain productivity and ensure the safety of agricultural products (Figure 4). The CRISPR-Cas system provides robust tools for achieving this objective through precise genome editing. A metallothionein gene (ScMT2-1-3), consisting of 700 and 240 bp open reading frames (ORF) that encode 79 amino acid residues (Guo et al., 2013), plays a critical role in copper detoxification. In wild sugar beets, genes such as BmMTP10, BmMTP11, NIC3, NIC6, NIC8, BvHMA3, and BvNRAMP3 are implicated in heavy metal stress tolerance (Erbasol et al., 2013; Bozdag et al., 2014; Haque et al., 2021), indicating potential target genes for CRISPR bases or prime editing to develop heavy metal-resistant sugar beet varieties.

In sweet sorghum, SbWRKY22 and SbWRKY65 transcripts were induced in the root apices under aluminum (Al) stress. These WRKY proteins are localized in the nucleus and exhibit transcriptional activity. Notably, SbWRKY22 played a significant role in regulating key genes associated with Al tolerance, whereas SbWRKY65 primarily affected the expression of SbWRKY22. This suggests that SbWRKY65 may indirectly regulate Al tolerance genes through SbWRKY22. These findings indicate the presence of pathways mediated by SbWRKY22 and SbWRKY65 that regulate Al tolerance in sweet sorghum (Guan et al., 2023). Furthermore, SbYS1 and the upstream transcription factor SbWRKY72 are crucial for cadmium (Cd) tolerance and accumulation in sweet sorghum (Jia et al., 2024). Taken together, genes including SbYS1 and SbWRKY72 have been identified through transcriptomic analysis in sweet sorghum under Cd stress and show homology to known metal tolerance genes. These represent hypothetical targets requiring experimental validation before CRISPR-mediated editing. Moreover, transcriptomic analysis revealed that Arg treatment significantly induced genes involved in GSH biosynthesis, polyamine metabolism and cell wall remodeling, including pathways related to pectin synthesis and lignin polymerization, thereby promoting Cd sequestration and strengthening the cell wall. (Ye et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). Furthermore, investigating the regulatory mechanisms of these genes using CRISPR/Cas9/12 and prime-editing tools will enhance heavy metal stress tolerance in sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum (Tables 1–3).

sec.title: Challenges and translational barriers
sec.p: Despite recent progress in genomics that sufficiently supports gene editing breeding (Supplementary Table S1), the actual deployment of CRISPR/Cas in sugar crops—predominantly sugarcane—faces a dominant translational bottleneck rooted in extremely low genetic transformation efficiency (Xia et al., 2018). Elite commercial sugarcane varieties display profound recalcitrance toward both A. tumefaciens mediated transformation and biolistic particle bombardment, with stable editing recovery rates of only 1%–5% across commercial varieties (Xia et al., 2018; Antony Ceasar and Ignacimuthu, 2023).This transformation barrier is multi-layered and genotype-dependent, driven by distinct physiological and epigenetic characteristics inherent to polyploid crops. Mature stalk and leaf explants show a limited capacity for embryogenic callus induction; ploidy-induced epigenetic silencing suppresses the uptake of exogenous DNA or RNP in proliferating cells; and tissue-specific cell wall rigidity hinders vector penetration during transfection. (Urnov et al., 2010). Combining low delivery and somatic regeneration pipeline of 6–12 months per editing event, a timeline far exceeding diploid model crops such as Arabidopsis and rice. Such prolonged culture cycles drastically inflate labor costs, slow germplasm screening, and delay multi-location field trail validation of stress-resistant edited lines. Even with haplotype-resolved gRNA design by sugarcane pangenome resources, the probability of isolating a uniform, heritable edited regenerant remains negligible without improvements to delivery workflows. Conceptually, advances in sugar crop pan-genomics and target gene identification have substantially advanced ‘which genes to modify’ challenge by enabling haplotype-aware guide design and the identification of stress-responsive gene families. However, the complexity of sugarcane’s auto-allopolyploid genome (∼10 Gb, 100–130 chromosomes), gene discovery remains an ongoing process, with many stress-responsive genes and regulatory networks yet to be fully characterized. Nevertheless, inefficient transformation and slow tissue culture regeneration create a persistent ‘how to deliver edits’ translation gap that remains the primary bottleneck for commercial deployment. Without transformative innovations in DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, lipid nanoparticle carriers, or plant viral vector transfection platforms, the full potential of CRISPR-engineered multi-stress resilient sugar varieties is challenging to be translated from lab experimentation to commercial breeding program. The application of CRISPR/Cas tools has attracted considerable interest to develop more resilient varieties. However, additional challenges beyond delivery also impede precise applications (Figure 5). The Cas9: gRNA complex can induce DNA breaks at off-target sites, potentially resulting in unintended mutations (Mall et al., 2024). The polyploid nature of sugar crops complicates mutant screening because numerous mutants are required for functional research. Moreover, high haplotype diversity means that multiple haplotypes exist for key agronomic genes (e.g., sucrose synthase), and editing a single copy often fails to produce a significant phenotype (Liu et al., 2023).

sec.p: CRISPR off-target occurrences arise due to partial base pairing between gRNA and non-target genomic protospacers, with Cas9 allowing up to 1–4 mismatches in the crucial PAM-proximal seed region of the RNA-DNA hybrid duplex (Sternberg and Doudna, 2015). This risk is significantly heightened in polyploid sugar crops, particularly sugarcane, 10 Gb auto-allopolyploid genome, numerous segmental duplications, repetitive intergenic sequences, and hundreds of paralogous stress gene haplotypes (Ou, 2026; Wang J. et al., 2026). The gRNAs that bind conserved regions shared across homologous sub-genomes frequently cause unintended double-strand breaks and indel mutations, with three major consequences for variety development. First, off-target disruption of key sucrose-metabolism or stress-related genes (SPS, WRKY, DREB) can both weaken the intended stress-tolerance phenotype and lower sucrose accumulation—directly undermining the crop’s primary economic value. yield in stalks and taproot tissues, thereby negating the primary economic trait of sugar crops. Second, unintended mutation of metal sequestration genes, such as ScMT2-1-3, results in increased accumulation of toxic heavy metals (Cu, Cd) in edible sink tissues, thereby breaching global safety standards for food and feed, particularly in industrial sucrose and bioethanol feedstock (Guo et al., 2013). Third, global regulatory frameworks for gene editing categorize heritable off-target variants as uncharacterized genomic alterations, necessitating expensive multi-generational whole-genome sequencing (WGS) validation to achieve variety registration (Liberty et al., 2025). In sugarcane, regeneration cycle for each edited event, comprehensive off-target screening significantly extends breeding timelines and elevates germplasm development costs. In polyploids, mosaic chimerism resulting from uneven off-target cleavage across divergent haplotypes further leads to inconsistent stress resistance phenotypes (Eid et al., 2021).

sec.title: Transformation and regeneration bottlenecks
sec.p: Polyploidy imposes two inherent molecular constraints that exacerbate the delivery bottleneck, which is absent in diploid model crops. First, sugarcane embryogenic callus cells exhibit ploidy-dependent epigenetic silencing pathways, which inhibit the stable nuclear uptake and retention of either plasmid CRISPR constructs or Cas9-gRNA ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) (Birch et al., 2010). This epigenetic suppression significantly reduces the proportion of callus that sustain functional editing machinery. Second, severe gene dosage imbalance across divergent haplotypes disrupts cellular reprogramming during somatic embryogenesis. Edited polyploid cells exhibit irregular mitotic division, prolonging full plant regeneration by an additional 3–6 months compared to diploid crops (Li and Iqbal, 2024; Mall et al., 2024). The combination of extremely low transformation recovery and extended tissue culture timelines impedes high-throughput screening of extensive stress-tolerant germplasm screening (Antony Ceasar and Ignacimuthu, 2023), even when gRNA sequences are fully optimized using haplotype-resolved pangenome assemblies.

sec.title: Functional redundancy and haplotype diversity
sec.p: Significant sequence divergence among paralogous gene haplotypes constitutes a translational barrier that is exclusive to polyploid sugar crops. In sugarcane, 71 distinct nsLTP haplotypes collectively regulate membrane stability under drought and chilling conditions (Li J. et al., 2022). Yet targeted editing of just one or two haplotypes rarely produces a detectable phenotype in transpiration control or cold acclimation, since the unedited paralogs continue to compensate functionally. Similar multi-copy redundancy is evident in sugar beet raffinose synthase (BvRS) and sweet sorghum salt-responsive WRKY genes. This genetic redundancy poses two primary challenges for breeding. First, custom multiplex gRNA cocktails must be developed to align with the unique single nucleotide polymorphism of each functional haplotype copy of a target gene (Kumbara et al., 2025). Second, high-depth next-generation sequencing genotyping is essential to verify uniform editing across at least three to five paralogous copies per regenerated plant, significantly increasing sequencing costs and screening efforts for breeding.

sec.title: DNA-Free RNP delivery
sec.p: CRISPR editing relies on plasmid vectors encoding Cas9 and gRNA sequences, which are delivered into plant cells and transcribed endogenously to assemble the editing complexes. In contrast, DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery directly introduces pre-assembled Cas9–guide RNA ribonucleoprotein complexes into sugar crop cells through biolistic bombardment, PEG-mediated protoplast transfection, or other membrane-permeabilization methods (Urnov et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2020). This technology is designed to fully eliminate exogenous DNA templates or expression plasmids, thereby preventing the integration of foreign genetic material into the sugar crop nuclear genomes. After cellular uptake, nuclear localization signals (NLS) fused to recombinant Cas9 guide the RNP complex into the nucleus, where gRNA hybridizes to the target protospacers and Cas9 catalyzes site-specific double-strand breaks (DSBs). A defining functional feature of RNPs is transient intracellular activity: unbound Cas9 protein and free gRNA are rapidly degraded by endogenous plant proteases and nucleases within 2–5 days post-transfection, with no sustained production of editing machinery across cell divisions (Eid et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2024; Mall et al., 2024; Brant et al., 2025).

Plasmid-based CRISPR systems drive continuous transcription of Cas9 and gRNA throughout regeneration period, leading to persistent DNA scanning across the repeat-dense auto-allopolyploid genome and frequent off-target double-strand breaks (DSBs) on homologous subgenomic paralogs (Ou, 2026; Wang J. et al., 2026). In contrast, pre-assembled RNPs remain biologically active inside cells for only 2–5 days before complete degradation by endogenous nucleases and proteases. This transient activity drastically limits the total number of gRNA-DNA binding events; comparative sugarcane protoplast trials under identical gRNA dosages confirm a significant reduction in detectable off-target variants using RNP delivery compared to plasmid-based systems (Wang Q. et al., 2021; Wu D. et al., 2026). Short-lived RNP exposure also eliminates uneven cleavage across divergent haplotypes, the primary source of mosaic chimerism described. Chimeric sugarcane plants produce inconsistent abiotic stress resistance and fail uniform multi-location field phenotyping trials, while RNP-derived regenerants exhibit uniform indel profiles across homologous gene copies. This consistent genotype substantially cuts labor expenditure and sequencing costs associated with multi-generational whole-genome sequencing (WGS) off-target screening. Agrobacterium-mediated and biolistic plasmid delivery often triggers random integration of vector backbones, antibiotic selection markers, and fragmented bacterial sequences into sugarcane chromosomes. These exogenous insertions can disrupt core agronomic regulators, including SPS, WRKY, DREB, and the heavy metal detoxification gene ScMT2-1-3, inadvertently impairing sucrose accumulation and stress tolerance phenotypes (Ferreira et al., 2012). DNA-free RNP workflows introduce no foreign DNA into plant cells, eliminating this secondary source of unplanned genomic damage in sugarcane, sugar beet, and sweet sorghum regenerants.

Global agricultural regulatory frameworks draw a definitive distinction between DNA-transgenic lines and transgene-free RNP-edited germplasm. Plasmid-modified sugarcane requires expensive, multi-year ecological and toxicology assessments alongside repeated multi-generational WGS validation to rule out foreign insertions and heritable off-target variants (Liberty et al., 2025). In contrast, transgene-free RNP lines qualify for streamlined approval pathways in China, the EU, the United States, and major sugar-producing nations such as Brazil. This regulatory shortcut shortens the timeline from lab editing to large-scale commercial cultivation by 3–5 years,an invaluable benefit given sugar crops protracted 6–12-month somatic regeneration cycle. Accelerated variety registration speeds the deployment of drought, salinity and heavy metal-tolerant germplasm onto marginal farmlands to sustain stable sucrose and bioethanol production.

sec.title: Haplotype-specific gRNA design
sec.p: Haplotype-aware gRNA engineering relies on high-quality haplotype-resolved genome assemblies and sugar crop graph pangenomes to distinguish sequence polymorphisms between divergent paralogous gene haplotypes (Liu et al., 2023; Bao et al., 2024; Healey et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). Unlike conventional universal gRNAs that bind conserved genomic regions shared across all homologs, the bioinformatic workflow selectively designs guide RNAs that exclusively hybridize to single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), small insertions or deletions (indels), and haplotype-unique motif signatures unique to one target gene copy (Sternberg and Doudna, 2015). Specialized computational framework, CRISPR-HAWK, demonstrated the feasibility of haplotype-aware gRNA design by integrating individual and population-scale variants into guide selection (Kumbara et al., 2025). However, CRISPR-HAWK was developed for human therapeutic applications using 1000 Genomes and gnomAD datasets, with validation on the human BCL11A sickle-cell locus. The conceptual framework is valuable for polyploid sugar crops, direct application to sugarcane require adaptation to incorporate crop-specific pangenome resources and account for the complexities of auto-allopolyploid genomes. Nevertheless, the underlying principle—using haplotype-specific genetic variation to guide gRNA design—remains highly relevant and can inform the development of similar pipelines for polyploid crops as phased pangenome resources become increasingly available. (Sternberg and Doudna, 2015; Huang et al., 2026). Without phased pangenome resources for large polyploid genomes, such as sugarcane, distinguishing haplotype-specific variants from inter-subgenome conserved sequences is computationally unfeasible, making this precision editing strategy inaccessible for unassembled polyploid germplasm (Liu et al., 2023; Pandey et al., 2025; Wang J. et al., 2026).

Haplotype-specific gRNA design enables locus-specific modification of individual gene copies without disrupting functionally valuable homologous haplotypes—a transformative advantage unique to polyploid sugarcane, sugar beet, and sweet sorghum (Liu et al., 2023; Todd et al., 2024; Dohm et al., 2025; Morris et al., 2026; Yanqing et al., 2026). Many elite sugarcane varieties carry coexisting haplotypes with opposing physiological functions: some paralogs negatively regulate abiotic stress tolerance, whereas alternate haplotypes support high sucrose biosynthesis under drought or saline conditions. Traditional non-specific gRNAs cleave every homologous copy simultaneously, abolishing both detrimental and beneficial gene activity and triggering severe pleiotropic yield losses alongside stress improvement. Targeted haplotype gRNAs allow breeders to precisely knockout or mutate only unfavorable stress-suppressing haplotypes while fully preserving intact wild-type alleles responsible for high sugar accumulation. This allele-selective editing eliminates unintended pleiotropic disruptions to sucrose metabolic pathways and avoids irreversible loss of native agronomic haplotypes that underpin commercial variety performance. In downstream breeding, this precision drastically reduces the volume of multi-location field phenotyping required to screen regenerants, as edited lines retain the full complement of favorable native alleles and display stable, predictable stress-resistance phenotypes without compromised biomass or sucrose yield. Additionally, haplotype-specific gRNA cocktails minimize genome-wide off-target DSBs by eliminating broad cross-paralog binding, lowering mandatory multi-generational whole-genome sequencing (WGS) validation costs.

While haplotype-aware gRNA engineering resolves the precision and functional redundancy barriers, it cannot mitigate the core delivery and regeneration bottlenecks. Even perfectly optimized, haplotype-exclusive gRNA sequences are impractical without efficient cellular delivery by biolistic, Agrobacterium or RNP workflows; superior guide design does not improve low transformation recovery rates or shorten the somatic regeneration timeline per edited event. Second major constraint stems from polyploid genomic complexity: stress tolerance traits are frequently governed by 3–5 or more functionally redundant haplotypes, each carrying distinct unique variants. Separate custom gRNAs must be synthesized for every target paralog to achieve uniform mutagenesis across all contributing copies, raising reagent costs and requiring complex multiplex transfection setups. Furthermore, post-editing high-depth NGS genotyping remains mandatory to verify complete modification of all intended haplotypes, even with optimized guide design, as variable cellular uptake of distinct gRNA molecules creates partial editing mosaic in polyploid callus. Finally, this strategy is entirely dependent on high-cost phased pangenome sequencing for each commercial sugarcane germplasm; un-sequenced elite varieties lack resolved haplotype variant data, rendering haplotype-specific gRNA design incredible for most non-sequenced breeding material.

sec.title: Comparative editing strategies for sugar crops
sec.p: The selection of an appropriate CRISPR strategy to improve abiotic stress tolerance in sugar crops requires careful consideration of several factors, including editing efficiency, heritability, off-target risk, and potential trade-offs with yield and sucrose accumulation rates. Knockout strategies (CRISPR/Cas9 and Cas12a) are the most effective for generating loss-of-function mutations in the negative regulators of stress tolerance. Unlike diploid model species, sugarcane (auto-allopolyploid), and sugar beet (amphidiploid) harbor multiple homoeologous copies of most stress-regulatory genes, meaning that single-gRNA knockouts often fail to elicit phenotypic shifts because unedited paralogs compensate through functional redundancy. However, in polyploid crops, such as sugarcane, functional redundancy across multiple homoeologs necessitates the simultaneous editing of multiple gene copies to achieve a measurable phenotype. For example, the 71 nsLTP genes/haplotypes in sugarcane exhibit extensive functional redundancy (Li J. et al., 2022), editing one or two copies often fails to produce significant improvements in membrane stability under drought stress. Successful knockout strategies require custom multiplex gRNA cocktails and high-depth sequencing to verify uniform editing across target copies per regenerated plant, which significantly increases screening costs and breeding timelines. Recent studies demonstrated the multiplex targeting in ​sugarcane, with co-editing of up to 40 copies of target genes, such as LIGULELESS1 (LG1), achieved through optimized gRNA design (Brant et al., 2024). Consequently, multiplexed NHEJ targeting all expressed copies is required for knockout strategies in sugarcane. However, this introduces distinct liabilities in repetitive polyploid genomes. The promoter editing approach offers a more nuanced strategy for modulating gene expression without completely abolishing the protein function. Stress-responsive gene expressions can be fine-tuned by introducing targeted mutations in cis-regulatory elements. Recent advances in massively parallel reporter assays in sorghum have demonstrated that compact deletions and targeted motif insertions in core promoter regions can enhance protein production 30-fold relative to that in the wild type (Groover et al., 2026). However, promoter editing requires detailed knowledge of regulatory elements and is technically more challenging than simple knockout approaches.

CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) and interference (CRISPRi) offer compelling alternatives for polyploid sugar crops because can modulate transcription without introducing DNA breaks, thereby circumventing mosaic indel profiles and structural rearrangements (Ding et al., 2022; Srithawong et al., 2026). By recruiting transcriptional effectors (VP64, VPR, or SunTag) to endogenous promoters, CRISPRa can upregulate stress-protective genes—such as BvHSF for heat tolerance or SsJAZ1 for drought signaling—while CRISPRi can repress negative regulators, such as SbWRKY50 (Alok et al., 2025). Because these systems do not alter the coding sequence, can reduce the risk of irreversible pleiotropic effects; if a yield penalty emerges, the transcriptional modulation can be reversed by segregating the dCas9 transgene or by employing transient ribonucleoprotein (RNP) activator complexes. Nevertheless, efficacy depends on chromatin accessibility and promoter conservation across haplotypes, which may necessitate haplotype-specific gRNA cocktails (Kumbara et al., 2025).

Base editing and prime editing occupy a precision niche distinct from NHEJ knockouts and transcriptional modulation. Cytosine and adenine base editors achieve direct C→T or A→G substitutions without DSBs, whereas prime editors combine Cas nickase with reverse transcriptase to introduce targeted insertions, deletions, or all types of point mutations via pegRNA guidance (Lin, 2026). In polyploids, these modalities are particularly valuable for engineering cis-regulatory SNPs or correcting dominant-negative variants without the collateral damage caused by multiplex NHEJ. Successful prime editing in hexaploid wheat, rice and potato demonstrates the feasibility of precise polyploid modification (Lin et al., 2020; Lin, 2026), although neither technology has yet been reported in sugarcane. A critical limitation is that each haplotype must be individually targeted if variants differ at the edit site, requiring high-depth amplicon sequencing to confirm uniform modifications across paralogs.​

sec.title: Polyploid constraints: Mosaics, partial alteration, and structural variation
sec.p: Genotype-dependent regeneration is the primary translational bottleneck. Elite commercial sugarcane varieties display profound recalcitrance toward Agrobacterium-mediated transformation and biolistic bombardment. This barrier is genotype-dependent and driven by ploidy-triggered epigenetic silencing of exogenous DNA or RNPs, as well as tissue-specific cell wall rigidity, which impedes vector penetration during transfection (Antony Ceasar and Ignacimuthu, 2023; Altpeter, 2025). The resulting somatic regeneration cycle per editing event far exceeds diploid models such as rice or Arabidopsis, drastically inflating labor costs and delaying germplasm screening (Brant et al., 2024; Altpeter, 2025; Brant et al., 2025; Wang W. et al., 2026). Editing mosaics and partial alteration of homologous copies are inevitable consequences of polyploidy. In sugarcane callus, uneven cleavage across divergent haplotypes produces chimeric plants. This mosaicism is invisible in shallow amplicon sequencing and is only revealed by high-depth long-read genotyping or phenotypic segregation in ratoon crops. Partial alteration of 1–2 copies in a 4x or 8x background typically yields no phenotypic shift due to dosage compensation; breeders must verify uniform editing across at least three to five paralogous copies per regenerated plant to breach the functional redundancy threshold. Additionally, capillary electrophoresis provides a cost-effective alternative to next-generation sequencing for detecting indel mosaicism in polyploid sugarcane (Eid et al., 2021; Altpeter, 2025; Brant et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).

On-target structural changes represent a severe but under a appreciated risk of multiplexed NHEJ in polyploid genomes. Simultaneous DSBs at adjacent target sites can generate large chromosomal deletions, inversions, and translocations between homoeologous chromosomes (Sturme et al., 2022). In poplar, multiplex editing of seven closely linked NRX1 genes induced diverse mutations, including translocations and inversions (Feng et al., 2025). In sugarcane’s ∼10 Gb auto-allopolyploid genome, harbors numerous segmental duplications and repetitive intergenic sequences, such structural variants can inadvertently disrupt sucrose phosphate synthase (SPS), WRKY, or DREB loci, negating the primary economic trait. Base and prime editing, which operate without DSBs, largely circumvent risk and should be prioritized when the breeding objective is a precise nucleotide change rather than gene elimination (Li et al., 2023; Wang T. et al., 2026).

sec.title: Pleiotropy, yield penalty and dosage sensitivity
sec.p: A critical but often overlooked consideration is the coupling of stress tolerance with yield or sucrose penalties. Stress-regulatory transcription factors are frequently embedded in hormones and metabolic networks that directly influence carbon partitioning. Constitutive overexpression of DREB1A confers drought, salt, and freezing tolerance but reduces plant growth, development, and reproduction by diverting carbon skeletons from biomass accumulation (Kasuga et al., 1999). Similarly, the constitutive activation of WRKY or HSF pathways may enhance antioxidant defense but impose a Brix penalty under non-stress conditions by repressing growth-promoting genes or exhausting cellular energy reserves.

Recent advances in promoter editing offer a route to decouple these traits. In maize, CRISPR-mediated insertion of drought-responsive cis-regulatory elements into the ARGOS8 promoter increased yield by up to five bushels per acre under drought without reducing yield under normal irrigation, demonstrating that tissue-specific or stress-inducible transcriptional tuning can improve resilience without an agronomic penalty (Shi et al., 2017). For sugar crops, analogous strategies—such as root-specific CRISPRa of BvDREB or stress-inducible activation of ScNsLTP promoters—may allow abiotic stress tolerance to be uncoupled from stalk sucrose content, though this hypothesis remains experimentally untested.

sec.title: Field validation and heritability
sec.p: Despite rapid progress in target identification and in vitro editing, no CRISPR-edited sugar crop has progressed to multi-location field trials for abiotic stress tolerance so far. Although field-validated CRISPR-edited maize (ZmHDT103) and rice (OsRR22) have demonstrated heritable stress resistance under multi-environment (Gao, 2021; Wang et al., 2024), equivalent validation in vegetatively propagated polyploid sugar crops is lacking. The sugarcane regeneration cycle, combined with ratoon propagation, needs to verify mitotic stability, that heredity of edited alleles remains uncharacterized in commercial germplasm. RNP-derived edits must be confirmed as stable through at least two vegetative generations, and stress phenotypes must be validated under field abiotic stress rather than in vitro or greenhouse conditions. Furthermore, global regulatory frameworks categorize heritable off-target variants as uncharacterized genomic alterations, necessitating expensive multi-generational whole-genome sequencing validation before variety registration (Liberty et al., 2025). Until field data and multi-generational inheritance studies are available, claims of “enhanced tolerance” in sugar crops remain pre-commercial hypotheses requiring rigorous phenotypic validation.

sec.title: Conclusion and future prospectives
sec.p: CRISPR-based systems offer substantial advantages over other genome-editing technologies because of their precision and user-friendly design. Recent achievements in targeting multiple gene copies in sugarcane underscore the feasibility of genome editing in polyploid crops, facilitating the development of varieties with improved tolerance to diverse abiotic and biotic stresses. CRISPR/Cas tools have significant potential for developing sugar beet breeding lines that exhibit resistance or tolerance to various abiotic and biotic stressors. By silencing or knocking out specific genes using CRISPR/Cas9/12, prime editors, and base editors, sugar beets can be engineered to adapt to challenging environmental conditions, thereby enhancing their physiological and biochemical stress tolerance. Furthermore, CRISPR-based methodologies enable the creation of novel traits via gain-of-function mutations, thereby contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of the gene regulatory networks involved in stress responses and supporting efforts to improve crops.

The application of CRISPR-based systems in sugarcane cultivation represents a significant advancement in agricultural biotechnology. Recent advancements in sugar crop genomics (e.g., reference genome availability, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and CRISPR/Cas reagent optimization- (Supplementary Table S1) have further enhanced its feasibility. These tools address longstanding challenges in sugar crop improvement under abiotic stress, offering a path toward sustainable, precision-bred varieties that maintain yield and quality even in adverse environmental conditions, meeting consumer and industrial demands. Furthermore, genome-editing research must address several challenges, including gene delivery issues, the risk of off-target effects, and the limited efficacy of current techniques. Despite these challenges, such research opens new avenues for sugar crop genome editing, potentially leading to a more resilient, productive, and sustainable agricultural future for sugar crops.
